section_titles: Tally marks as a counting strategy
periods.activity_title: Marks on the Wall, Letters in a Name

tasks_in_class.description: Help Hemant keep track of his 36 cows and 23 sheep by making marks like Deba and Deep.
Find the animal with the most letters (first-team captain) and fewest letters (second-team captain) from: tiger, elephant, deer, rat, monkey, ox, dog, snake, goat, lion.

Write friends' names; tick longest and cross shortest; find starting letter of own name; count names with same starting letter; find most-used starting letter; count names with same ending letter; write letters not used as starting letters.

time_bands.activity: Read aloud the story of Deba and Deep tracking cows with wall marks. Students make tally marks on their slates or paper: one stroke per cow going out, struck through on return. Then they complete p.2 ("Help Hemant keep track of his 36 cows and 23 sheep by making marks like Deba and Deep."), experiencing one-to-one correspondence concretely before any numeral is written.

Students count the letters in each animal name on Let us Do Q1, p.3 ("Find the animal with the most letters..."), arranging names from longest to shortest. Pairs compare their rankings and resolve any disagreement by re-counting together, building the idea that letter-count is a measurable, comparable quantity.

Students carry out Let us Do Q3, p.4 ("Write friends' names; tick longest and cross shortest; find starting letter..."), collecting names from neighbours and analysing starting and ending letters. The teacher draws attention to patterns that emerge — which letters appear most often, which not at all — inviting children to notice that a familiar set of words can yield surprising structure.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error at this stage is counting a hyphen or space in a compound word as a letter — remind children that only alphabet letters are counted, not punctuation or gaps. Let us Do Q2, p.3 ("Who has a longer name — Mahesh or Kartik?") covers the same single-comparison act as Q1; it may be offered as quick oral practice or an early-finisher task rather than a separate class activity.
materials: Slates or rough paper for tally marks

periods.activity_title: How Many Letters Hide in a Number?

tasks_in_class.description: Write some numbers and their number names in your notebook; count how many letters each has.
Write other numbers between 1 and 99 that have 8 letters (given that fifty-six = 8 letters).
Write the number(s) between 1 and 99 that have the longest name.

homework.description: Write your roll number using number cards as shown; count how many letters its number name has.

time_bands.activity: Students open notebooks and carry out Let us Do Q4(b), p.5 ("Write some numbers and their number names in your notebook; count how many letters each has."), choosing at least six numbers across the range 1–99. The teacher circulates, checking that children spell out the full number name before counting, and notes on the board any interesting totals that come up.

The class tackles Let us Think, p.5 ("Write other numbers between 1 and 99 that have 8 letters..."), starting from the given anchor 'fifty-six'. Students work in pairs, systematically checking number names, and share their lists. The teacher invites the class to notice which tens-families tend to produce eight-letter names, building the habit of pattern-search over brute enumeration.

Students investigate Let us Do Q1, p.6 ("Write the number(s) between 1 and 99 that have the longest name."), now applying the same systematic approach to a new constraint. Small groups pool their findings and the class settles on a verified answer, with the teacher prompting: 'How do you know you haven't missed one?'

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error here is omitting the hyphen-separated second word from a compound name like 'forty-three' — children count only 'forty' and get 5 instead of 11. Reinforce that the full spelled-out name, including the word after the hyphen, is what is counted. Let us Do Q4(a), p.5, which uses roll-number cards, is a brief personal version of Q4(b) and is well-suited as homework so every child can use their own number.
materials: Number-name word cards (optional, from textbook or hand-made)

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do Q2 Find out (left), p.6
tasks_in_class.description: My number name has two words; first word 6 letters, second word 5 letters; I am very near to 100. Who am I?

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do Q2 Find out (right), p.6
tasks_in_class.description: My friends and I are the numbers from 63 to 78; my number name is the smallest among all my friends. Who am I?
Make similar number-name puzzles of your own in your notebook and ask your classmates.

time_bands.activity: The class reads and works through Let us Do Q2 Find out (left), p.6 ("My number name has two words; first word 6 letters, second word 5 letters; I am very near to 100."). Students list two-word number names near 100, count the letters in each word, and narrow down to the answer. The teacher models thinking aloud: 'Near 100 means nineties — let me check each one.'

Students tackle Let us Do Q2 Find out (right), p.6 ("My friends and I are the numbers from 63 to 78; my number name is the smallest among all my friends."). Working individually, they write all number names from 63 to 78, count each name's letters, and identify the one with the fewest. Pairs swap work and verify each other's counts before the class agrees on an answer.

Students compose their own number-name puzzles as in Let us Do Q3, p.6 ("Make similar number-name puzzles of your own..."), writing at least two clue-sets in their notebooks. They then swap puzzles with a neighbour and solve each other's, giving the puzzle-maker immediate feedback on whether the clues are precise enough to have a unique answer.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes interpret 'smallest name' as the smallest number rather than the shortest name — draw attention to the distinction by asking 'Are we looking for a small number or a name with few letters?' before they begin. The puzzle-posing task in Let us Do Q3, p.6 also functions as a check on understanding: a child who can write an unambiguous puzzle has genuinely grasped how letter-count constrains number identity.

tasks_in_class.description: Write TV, Lamp, Clock, Pillow, Chair, Bed, Blanket, Fan into two groups: things that need electricity and things that don't need electricity.
Group the same objects differently using your own criterion; write them in the space below.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do Hair Styles, p.8
tasks_in_class.description: Look at children in your class; observe how each child has combed their hair; fill the hair-style vs number-of-children table.

time_bands.activity: Students read the story of Teji's grouping and Jojo's regrouping in the textbook, then complete Let us Do Q4, p.7 ("Write TV, Lamp, Clock, Pillow, Chair, Bed, Blanket, Fan into two groups: things that need electricity and things that don't."). The teacher asks: 'What rule did you use?' after everyone has written their groups, establishing that a rule must be clear and must account for every item.

Students re-examine the same eight objects and invent their own grouping criterion for Let us Do (group differently), p.8 ("Group the same objects differently using your own criterion."). Volunteers share their criteria; the class tests each proposed rule against all eight items. The teacher highlights that the same set of objects can be sorted in many valid ways, building the core insight of this section.

Students conduct a quick classroom survey for Let us Do Hair Styles, p.8 ("Look at children in your class; observe how each child has combed their hair; fill the hair-style vs number-of-children table."), using tally marks to record observations as they walk around briefly, then converting tallies to counts and filling the table. The teacher links this directly back to the tally-mark idea from the chapter's opening story, showing that counting strategies carry through into data collection.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent error in classification tasks is placing an object in both groups or leaving one out — remind students that every item must belong to exactly one group under the chosen rule, and none may be skipped. The hair-styles survey gives an excellent opportunity to ask 'How did you keep track without losing count?' connecting back to the tally-mark strategy that opened the chapter.
materials: Chalk or a class display space for tally counts

items.section_title: Tally marks as a counting strategy
items.prompt: A farmer has 14 goats. Each morning he makes one tally mark as each goat goes out to graze. By noon, 9 goats have returned and he strikes out a mark for each one. Draw the tally marks on the farmer's wall at noon, showing which goats are still out.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The wall should show 14 tally marks in total; 9 of them struck through (crossed out), and 5 marks left uncrossed, representing the 5 goats still out grazing.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Make one mark per goat going out, then strike through one mark for each goat that returns.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child use counters or fingers to act it out; stretch: ask them to show what the wall looks like after 2 more goats return.

exercise.description: Help Hemant keep track of his 36 cows and 23 sheep by making marks like Deba and Deep.

items.prompt:
Priya is looking at the children in her class. She notices that some children have braided hair and some have open hair. There are 7 children with braided hair and 11 children with open hair. Use tally marks to show Priya's count for each hair style in the table below.

| Hair Style | Tally Marks | Number of Children |
| Braided | | 7 |
| Open | | 11 |
items.visual_stimulus:
| Hair Style | Tally Marks | Number of Children |
| Braided | | 7 |
| Open | | 11 |

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Braided row: tally marks showing 7 (five-bar gate plus two single marks); Open row: tally marks showing 11 (two five-bar gates plus one single mark).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw one tally mark per child, grouping in sets of five with a cross-stroke, then count the marks to verify they match the number given.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child tap a finger for each count and draw marks one at a time; stretch: ask them to add a third hair style with 8 children and draw its tally marks too.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Do Hair Styles, p.8
exercise.description: Look at children in your class; observe how each child has combed their hair; fill the hair-style vs number-of-children table.

items.prompt: Count the letters in each animal name: parrot, bee, crocodile, frog. Which animal has the most letters in its name?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: crocodile — it has 9 letters, more than parrot (6), bee (3), and frog (4).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the letters in each name one by one, then compare the totals to find the largest.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have chosen the first option without counting all names, or miscounted 'parrot' as more than 6.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may have confused 'shortest' with 'longest', selecting the name with the fewest letters.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may have stopped comparing after checking only 'parrot' and 'frog', missing 'crocodile'.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child write out each name and underline letters one by one before comparing; stretch: ask which two animals together have the same total letters as crocodile.

exercise.description: Find the animal with the most letters (first-team captain) and fewest letters (second-team captain) from: tiger, elephant, deer, rat, monkey, ox, dog, snake, goat, lion.

items.prompt: Here are four names: Riya, Arjun, Meena, Om. Write them in order from shortest name (fewest letters) to longest name (most letters). If two names have the same number of letters, write them next to each other.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Om (2 letters), Riya (4 letters), Arjun (5 letters), Meena (5 letters). Arjun and Meena may appear in either order since both have 5 letters.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the letters in each name, then arrange the counts from smallest to largest.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child write each name and number each letter underneath before ordering; stretch: ask them to write one more name that fits between Om and Riya in length.

exercise.description: Write friends' names; tick longest and cross shortest; find starting letter of own name; count names with same starting letter; find most-used starting letter; count names with same ending letter; write letters not used as starting letters.

items.prompt: The number name 'fifty-six' has 8 letters (f-i-f-t-y-s-i-x, not counting the hyphen). Which of the following number names also has exactly 8 letters?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 'sixty-five' has 8 letters: s-i-x-t-y-f-i-v-e — wait, that is 9. Re-verification: sixty (5) + five (4) = 9. Forty (5) + five (4) = 9. Twenty (6) + one (3) = 9. Thirty (6) + two (3) = 9. Sixty (5) + five (4) = 9.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: [Verification failed] Refer to the book task anchored to S3.

exercise.description: Write other numbers between 1 and 99 that have 8 letters (given that fifty-six = 8 letters).

items.prompt: Write the number names for 85, 90, and 99. Count the letters in each (do not count hyphens). Which of these three number names has the most letters? Write your answer and show your counting.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: eighty-five: e-i-g-h-t-y-f-i-v-e = 10 letters. ninety: n-i-n-e-t-y = 6 letters. ninety-nine: n-i-n-e-t-y-n-i-n-e = 10 letters. Both 'eighty-five' and 'ninety-nine' have 10 letters; either is a correct answer for most letters, or the child may say they are equal.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Spell out each number name fully, count each letter one by one ignoring hyphens, then compare the totals.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write the number names on the board and let the child point and count aloud; stretch: ask them to find one more two-digit number whose name also has 10 letters.

exercise.description: Write the number(s) between 1 and 99 that have the longest name.

items.prompt:
Here are clues about a mystery number. Read them carefully and write the number.
• My number name has two words.
• The first word has 6 letters.
• The second word has 4 letters.
• I am between 90 and 100.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: ninety-four. 'ninety' has 6 letters; 'four' has 4 letters; 94 is between 90 and 100.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List two-word number names between 90 and 100, count the letters in each word, and match to the clues.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write the number names from 91 to 99 on the board and let the child count letters in each word; stretch: ask them to write their own two-clue puzzle for a number between 80 and 90.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Do Q2 Find out (left), p.6
exercise.description: My number name has two words; first word 6 letters, second word 5 letters; I am very near to 100. Who am I?

items.prompt: Rahul sorts these objects into two groups using the rule 'needs electricity / does not need electricity': torch, book, mixer, pencil, fan, eraser. How many objects are in the group that needs electricity?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3. The objects that need electricity are: torch, mixer, fan. Book, pencil, and eraser do not need electricity.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Go through each object, decide whether it needs electricity to work, place it in the correct group, and count the objects in the electricity group.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may have omitted one electrical object, perhaps not classifying torch as needing electricity.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may have incorrectly included one non-electrical object such as book or pencil in the electricity group.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have placed most objects in the electricity group, leaving only one in the other group.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to say aloud whether each object is plugged in or uses a battery before placing it; stretch: ask them to invent a different rule to re-sort the same six objects into two groups.

exercise.description: Write TV, Lamp, Clock, Pillow, Chair, Bed, Blanket, Fan into two groups: things that need electricity and things that don't need electricity.

items.prompt: Look at these six things: apple, stone, candle, leaf, ice cream, feather. Your friend sorted them using the rule 'can melt / cannot melt'. Write which objects go in each group. Then write a different rule of your own and sort the same objects into two groups using that rule.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Can melt: candle, ice cream. Cannot melt: apple, stone, leaf, feather. For the student's own rule, any clear criterion that places all six objects into exactly two groups is acceptable — e.g. 'found in nature / made by people', 'heavy / light', 'has colour / no colour'. The teacher checks that every object appears in exactly one group.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the given rule to each object one at a time, then repeat with the student's own rule ensuring every object is placed.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: discuss each object aloud before writing — 'Does a candle melt when it gets hot?'; stretch: ask whether there is any object that could reasonably go in either group depending on how the rule is worded, and discuss why.

exercise.description: Group the same objects differently using your own criterion; write them in the space below.

items.prompt: Count the letters in the number name 'thirty-seven' (do not count the hyphen). How many letters does it have?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Spell out each word of the number name, count the letters in each word separately, then add the two counts.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may have counted only one of the two words, getting 5 (seven) + 4 = 9, or miscounted 'thirty' as 4 letters.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student likely counted 'thirty' correctly as 6 but undercounted 'seven' as 4, giving 10.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have counted a space or hyphen as a letter, adding 1 extra to the correct total of 11.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write 'thirty' and 'seven' separately and let the child number each letter beneath it; stretch: ask them to find another two-digit number whose name also has 11 letters.

exercise.description: Write some numbers and their number names in your notebook; count how many letters each has.
